body_html:
A mobile SEO platform is any tool, or set of tools, that shows how your site performs for people and search engines on phones: how Google crawls the mobile version, how fast pages load and respond, and where you rank in mobile results. The right one depends on your site's size and how you report.

There's no single product that does everything. Most teams combine free Google tools with one or two paid tools. This post explains what to look for so you can compare options on features that matter instead of on marketing pages.

Why does mobile SEO need its own tools?

Google indexes and ranks the mobile version of your pages. Its documentation on mobile-first indexing best practices says Google uses the mobile version of a site's content, crawled with its smartphone crawler, for indexing and ranking. If something is missing or broken on mobile, Google may not see it, even if the desktop page looks fine.

That means the questions you need answered are mobile-specific:

  • Does the mobile page have the same main content, headings, structured data, and meta tags as desktop?
  • How fast does it load and respond on real phones?
  • Where do you rank when someone searches from a phone, often from a specific location?

Some older tools you may remember are gone. Google retired its Mobile-Friendly Test and Search Console's Mobile Usability report in December 2023, as announced on the Search Central blog, and pointed people to Lighthouse instead. If a vendor or checklist still points you there, it's out of date.

What should a mobile SEO platform do?

Use these features as your comparison checklist. A strong setup covers all of them, whether through one tool or several.

1. Crawl as a smartphone

The crawler should be able to fetch pages using a smartphone user agent (the label a browser or bot uses to say what device it is) and render JavaScript the way a modern browser does. Without rendering, you can miss content and links that only appear after scripts run.

2. Compare mobile and desktop versions

If your site serves different content to phones, through dynamic serving or a separate mobile site, you need a way to spot gaps: missing text, different titles, dropped structured data, or robots meta tags that don't match. If your site is fully responsive, this matters less, but it's still worth checking templates that hide content on small screens.

3. Report Core Web Vitals from real users

Core Web Vitals are Google's three page experience measurements: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) for loading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) for responsiveness, and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) for visual stability. INP replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in March 2024, so any tool still reporting FID as a core metric is behind.

Look for tools that show field data, meaning measurements from real visitors, not only lab tests run in a simulated browser. Google's Core Web Vitals report in Search Console uses real-user data, reports mobile and desktop separately, and lists the thresholds for "good": LCP within 2.5 seconds, INP within 200 milliseconds, and CLS of 0.1 or less.

4. Track mobile rankings by location

Mobile and desktop results can differ, and local results change from one neighborhood to the next. A useful rank tracker lets you choose device type and location for each keyword. If you serve a specific area, this matters more than tracking hundreds of national terms. If you'd rather not manage it yourself, see my keyword tracking service.

5. Connect to Search Console and GA4

Search Console is the only place you'll see Google's own data on clicks, impressions, and indexing for your site. GA4 shows what mobile visitors do after they arrive. A platform that pulls from both, or exports cleanly into Data Studio (formerly Looker Studio), saves time and keeps everyone looking at the same numbers.

6. Prioritize issues, not just list them

Long lists of warnings aren't helpful on their own. Look for tools that group issues by template or page type, show how many pages each problem affects, and let you mark items as fixed so you can track progress.

7. Fit your size and team

A ten-page local site and a large online store need different things. Check crawl limits, how many projects or keywords you can track, user seats, and whether you can schedule recurring crawls. More features don't help if nobody has time to use them.

Which tools make up a typical mobile SEO platform?

Most mobile SEO setups combine a few categories of tools:

Tool typeExamplesWhat it answers
Google's free toolsSearch Console, PageSpeed Insights, Lighthouse in Chrome DevToolsHow Google sees your pages, real-user Core Web Vitals, lab performance audits
Site crawlersScreaming Frog, SitebulbTechnical issues across every page, mobile rendering, structured data
SEO suitesSemrush, AhrefsMobile rankings, competitors, site audits, keyword research
ReportingData Studio, GA4Combined dashboards and what visitors do after they land

These are examples, not endorsements. Feature sets change often, so confirm current capabilities in each tool's documentation or a free trial before you commit.

How do you choose the right mobile SEO platform?

  1. Start with the free Google tools. Search Console and PageSpeed Insights show you whether mobile problems exist before you spend anything.
  2. List your actual questions. Is it slow pages, missing mobile content, or not knowing where you rank on phones? Pick tools that answer those first.
  3. Test on your own site. Use a trial to crawl your real pages and see whether the findings are clear and accurate.
  4. Check the reporting. Make sure the data can reach the people who need it, in a format they'll read.
  5. Plan who will act on it. A tool finds problems; someone still has to fix templates, images, and scripts.

Is Google Search Console enough for mobile SEO?

For small sites, it covers a lot: indexing, real-user Core Web Vitals, and search performance you can filter by device. What it doesn't do is crawl every page on demand, compare mobile and desktop versions side by side, or track rankings by location. Most growing sites add a crawler and a rank tracker once Search Console points to problems worth investigating.

Do you still need to test mobile usability now that Google's test is gone?

Yes. The tool was retired, not the need. Use Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools for lab checks, test key pages on real phones, and watch Search Console's Core Web Vitals report for real-user data. Pay attention to tap targets, text size, pop-ups that cover content, and forms that are hard to complete on a small screen.

How often should you run mobile SEO checks?

Check Search Console weekly or monthly, depending on how often your site changes. Run a full crawl after any redesign, migration, theme update, or new plugin, since those are common times for mobile issues to appear. Core Web Vitals data in Search Console is based on real visits over time, so give changes a few weeks before judging results.
